title: Two Words Make One
objectives: I can say that two small words can make one new word.
I can find the two small words inside playground, rainbow, backpack, butterfly, and bedtime.
I can tell what each compound word means.
rationale: Children see that a long word can be split into two small words they already know, which makes long words less scary and starts their word study. The five examples come from places and times in their own day, such as the playground, backpack, and bedtime. Butterfly is included on purpose as a caution: its two parts are real words, but they do not tell the meaning, so children learn to check the meaning and not only the parts. The unit revisits climb, ready, and neighbor.

passage.title: Zoe's Good Day

Zoe says it was the best day. She falls asleep with a smile.

look: tells what the big word means
constructed.model: Backpack is back and pack. A backpack is a bag you carry on your back.

teacher.overview: Children learn that two small words can make one new word by cutting words apart with their hands, then hear all five words in a short story about a girl's day. The unit is oral; children say the parts and the whole word.

notes.va.playground.n: Use two index cards, one with a picture of play and one of ground, and slide them together. Check that children know ground. The word is a place outside, so contrast with a classroom.
notes.va.rainbow.n: Rain plus bow works for meaning because a rainbow is a bow of color after rain. Children may know bow as a ribbon; show a curve to match the sense. Keep science light: a rainbow shows when sun and rain are together.
notes.va.backpack.n: Back plus pack works for the whole meaning, so this is the best first example. Have children point to their back and hold a pack. Review ready by asking what goes in your backpack to be ready.
notes.va.butterfly.n: Butter plus fly is a caution: the two small words are real, but a butterfly is not butter that flies. Teach to check meaning, not just parts. Do not say anything about where the name came from unless you are sure.
notes.va.bedtime.n: Bed plus time works well and ties to routines. Children enjoy telling their own bedtime steps. Be sensitive that bedtimes differ at home.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'This long word is backpack. I can cut it in two. Back. Pack. A pack on your back! Backpack means a bag you carry on your back. Now I check: does butterfly work? Butter and fly. A butterfly is not butter. So I have to check the meaning too.'
discuss: What other word can you make with time or ground?
Which word did the two small words help you understand the most?
misconceptions: Every long word can be cut into two small words that tell its meaning.
A butterfly is butter that can fly.
The two small words always go in the same order.
extend: Make a class chart of compound words with two pictures each, such as sun and flower.
Go on a compound-word hunt in the room: classroom, notebook, bookshelf.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit climb, ready, and neighbor by asking children to use each in a sentence with a compound word, such as 'I climb on the playground.' Use compound ideas again in later grades when word parts get more complex.

frames: A backpack is a bag you carry on your ___.
wida.oral: Partner A says two small words, such as rain and bow. Partner B says the big word, rainbow, and tells what it is. Then they switch roles.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (patio de recreo, arcoíris, mochila, mariposa, la hora de dormir) have not been reviewed by a native speaker; playground varies by region (patio, parque infantil, área de juegos) and bedtime is a phrase.
Morphology: butterfly's segments butter + fly are real words and spell the headword, but the unit does not claim they explain the name; the origin of the word is intentionally not stated.
Sense boundary: rainbow's bow is glossed as a curved shape; no origin is claimed.
Spanish compound words are formed differently, so the two-small-words idea may not carry over for multilingual learners; arcoíris is a compound but mariposa is not.
